THE characters of the stalk are as strongly hereditary as are the characters of the ear. The first step, therefore, in improving corn in any given locality is to select in the field strong stalks, free from shakes and weakness, broad leaves and plenty of brace roots; ears not too high from the ground, with moderately long shank and a heavy shuck, completely drawn over the end of the ear. IN BRUSSELS, King Leopold
died at 2:35 o'clock this morning, his
aged and wasted body being unable to
stand the strain put upon it. The collapse occurred suddenly, and at a moment when the doctors seemingly had
the greatest hopes for his recovery.
Throughout yesterday bulletins indicated
progressive improvement. The bulletin
posted at 5:00 o'clock gave the king:
temperature, pulse and respiration as
practically normal. Apparently the
drainage of the wound was perfect, as
no fever was present all day. The
king had been able to take some nourishment.

The public at large was satisfied that
the king was on the road to recovery,
but within the pavilion where the king lay there was feeling of anxiety,
chiefly because of Leopold's great age.
After a restful day the patient was
able to sleep for a brief period early
in the evening and tonight passed quiet.

Approach of Death.
But towards midnight alarming symptoms
appeared. Suddenly the king
stirred and called to Dr. Thirar:
"Etouffe, docteur, etouffe,
I'm suffering."

Dr. De Page was summoned and the
two physicians did everything possible
to prolong life, but without avail.
The end came quickly and, after a
spell of weakness, peacefully. Prince
Albert arrived at the death-bed about
twenty-five minutes later.

He was accompanied by Princess
Clementine. Albert kissed the dead
king, and left the chamber weeping.
Baron Goffinet, the king's secretary,
started immediately for Brussels to notify members of the royal family. As
he was entering his motor car, he exclaimed:

"To think that only yesterday we
were still full of confidence and now
the king is dead."

Physicians Surprised.
It appears that the doctors were totally unprepared for fatal termination.

It was a nun, acting as nurse, who first
noticed the heavy breathing of the
king.

She called Dr. Thirar to the bedside.
Doctors Thirar and De Page resorted
to injections of morphine, but these had
no effect.

Soon after the end had come the ministers were notified. The first official
to arrive at the death chamber was
the royal chaplain. The ministers re-
plained in the chamber for considerable
time discussing in subdued tones the
sudden death and matters of state.

The king's goodness and courage in
the heroic struggle won the admiration
of all. For at no time did he seem to
fear the result. Now that he is dead
it is believed that he was able to survive so long by the sheer force of his
mentality.

When Goffinet emerged from the high
walls of the royal gardens his pale face
startled the newspaper correspondents
outside. He paused for a moment and
said solemnly, "The king is dead."

Biographical Sketch.
Leopold II, king of the Belgians,
son of the late King Leopold I, upon
whose death on December 10, 1865, he
succeeded to the throne, was born at
Brussels, April 9, 1835. His father was
a former Prince of Saxe-Coburg-Gotha,
and his mother Princess Louise, daughter
of King Louis Philippe of France.

On August 26, 1853, he married the
Archduchess Marie Henrietta, daughter
of Archduke Joseph of Austria. She
died September 30, 1902. There were
three daughters born of this union.

SPECIAL EDITION


LONG BEACH, Dec. 26,—In a cave
in the bluff along the ocean shore
Robert Allen, a nomadic individual
whose snowy hair and beard are of
patriarchal appearance, was arrested
last night by Detective O'Rourke and
was given a ten-day sentence in the
county Jail on a charge of vagrancy.
It is said that the old man has
begged for food at intervals for more
than a month in the Alamitos bay district. An elderly woman said the man
had bothered her and that she was
frightened by his visits. The police
had received several reports regarding
Allen and yesterday determined to locate him. Detective O'Rourke received
reports of his visits in several different quarters, and finally traced the
aged man to his bed in a cave in the
bluff. Allen was asleep and the embers of a fire showed where he had
warmed up a frugal evening meal. His
bed was the ground, and a sack his pillow.


The old man said little to the police
regarding his past, but indicated that
he had been well-to-do at one time
but had lost his small fortune through
a supposed friend's deceitfulness.


"We had a pretty hard time of it
and the air is somewhat cool and sharp
at nights," he said. "Perhaps I ought
to be thankful for a ten-day jail sentence as a Christmas gift. At least I
will be warmly housed and fed, and
that is a hard problem for a homeless
old man like me."

WEST POINT, June 11.—In an address at the graduation of the class of 1909 at the military academy this afternoon, Secretary of War Dickinson said:

Today the eyes of our people are turned to you with profound interest, hope and confidence. The fire broke out on the third floor of the building at about 8 o'clock, and with incredible swiftness swept the entire length of the building, breaking through the roof and leaping to the adjoining Luna boarding house. The entire force of the department, with all apparatus, responded to the general alarm, but it was not until after 10 o'clock, after almost two hours of strenuous efforts by the firefighters, that the flames were extinguished and the levee given.

The origin of the fire is attributed to either defective wiring or the overturning of a firepot used by one of the workmen engaged on the third floor.

The floor on which the fire originated was used chiefly for storage purposes practically its whole space being taken up with wrapped and grated stock, thus providing an abundance of inflammable material in the shape of burlap, excelsior and paper. Electricians were working on the floor at the time of the fire and one supposition is that one of the men may have overturned a firepot setting fire to the excelsior or packing. Another theory is that sparks from short circuit or crossed wires started the blaze.

Firemen Are Quick.

With the first shoot of flame the electricians ran from the floor, giving the alarm, and two calls were sent in to the fire department central station. In less than five minutes the entire department was at the scene of the fire, with twelve lines of hose and two steamers pouring perfect deluge of water upon the flames. Before the department arrived, however, the flames had eaten their way through the roof and were threatening the adjoining buildings.

Fire Chief W. H. Glore personally directed the fight against the flames, and quickly placed his men with their streams to the best advantage. The fire had begun in the southwest corner of the building, about fifty feet from the front, and spread to the rear. With quick realization of the dangers, Chief Glore's first work was to see that all drafts were shut off as much as possible and the fire was fought from the north toward the south, forcing the flames in the latter direction and preventing spread.

The firemen were forced to chop their way through this mass, and a considerable delay in forcing their way to the seat of the fire resulted.

Through the work of the department the actual fire was confined mainly to the third floor and the roof. The stock stored on the third floor was completely destroyed by the fire, but a greater damage was done by water to the stocks on the lower floors.

Spectacular Scene.

The fire was hazardous and dangerous to combat, not only by reason of its location, but also on account of the dense smoke and the fumes which arose from burning varnished and lacquered furniture. With the shooting flames cleaning through the veil of smoke the sight was a spectacular one and drew an immense throng of onlookers. The utmost efforts of the police department were required to keep the crowd outside the fire lines.

The building is owned by the I Y L Furniture company. It has a frontage of 20 feet and a depth of 80 feet. The insurance on the stock was divided among over seventy companies for the reason that no company will accept risk of over $5,500 on furniture stocks.

The work of the department in controlling and subduing the fire brought out much commendation. dishes may be made from the fol
lowing reliable formula If the pro-

followed. The ingredients required
are:


One quart of sifted -four.


Five teaspoonfuls of baking pow

Half cupful of butter.

small pieces. add salt and sugar
The ingredients must be thoroughly
rubbed together with the hands,
rubbing the butter well into the
-four. Lastly add the milk and then
handle as little as possible. With
this dough any of the following
dishes may be made:
Tea Biscuit.
Place the dough on mixing
board, fatten with the hand until
an inch in thickness. Do not use
the rolling pin. Cut in desired size
with a biscuit cutter and bake in
moderate oven from 20 minutes
to half an hour.


Dutch Rolls.


Roll the dough until it Is half an
inch thick. Dot with small bits of
butter half an inch apart Sprinkle
generously with sugar and roll Cut
in slices about an inch thick ana
bake in hot oven for half an hour.


Raisin Loaf.


Make the mixture as directed, but
add half a pound of raisins before
adding the milk. Then bake in a
bread tin in slow oven for three
quarters Of an hour.


Shortcake.


Mix as directed, then bake in a
round tin for half an hour. Split the
cakes and butter them while hot.
Place layer of fruit or preserves
between them and serve with sifted
sugar and whipped cream.


Roly-Poly Pudding.


Mix as directed, roll the dough
until about half an inch thick, then
cover with fresh fruit and roll 1t
up. Place in a granite dish or
earthen bowl and steam for half an
hour. If preferred the dough may
be covered with jam or jelly, and,
after being rolled up tightly, baked
for three-quarters of an hour.


Pie Crust.


This mixture will also make a
good plain pie crust and is espe-
cially good when making meat pies.

Mr. Cowles' communication follows: The express system of discriminating in favor of large towns against small towns, of large dealers against small dealers, is clearly set forth by the Interstate Commerce Commission in the case of "The Boise Commercial Club of Boise, Idaho, vs. The Adams Express Co. and others" decided June 24, 1909.

When either the point of origin or destination is an exclusive office of one express company, collect parcel pays as many different rates as there are lines that handle it. When the entire service between the points of origin and destination is operated by a single company or by each of two or more companies, the "collect" parcel pays but one rate though handled by each of the different companies in its transit. These express rules apply to all collect parcels and to all parcels whether the charges be prepaid or collected, but prepaid parcels up to 25 pounds dispatched by manufacturers and dealers who give the express companies large and continuous shipments enjoy special rate of one cent per ounce, the charge in no case to be less than 15 cents per package.

These special rates, however, are forbidden to packages forwarded by transient shippers.

Boise is an exclusive office of the Pacific Express Co., but New York City is not favored with its service. A pound collect parcel from New York to Boise is therefore taxed 20 cents by whomsoever dispatched and the parcel of the ordinary New York citizen pays the same rate whether the charge be prepaid or collected. To the Editor of The Robesonian:


I've been writing for The Robesonian, off and on, now for nearly forty years, and if I should perchance repeat myself, and if any of your readers have lived that long, I beg them not to criticise; for even Homer is said to have nodded, and the idea that Shakespeare has never repeated himself is all a farce.


I don't suppose there is a reader through the whole of The Robesonian's circulation that has ever read enough of the classics to know whether any of them have ever repeated themselves or not. We don't read the best of literature these days, but confine ourselves mostly to the latest highly-advertised novels. Of the old masters of fiction and poetry we used to get an inkling in our school days, and if we don't do it then we never will. A man will have to be a recluse if he reads anything substantial these days. We are getting to be a nation of newspaper readers, and this style of reading unites one for solid and substantial literature.


The above stuff, after reading it over, reminds the writer of DR. Kingsbury's style, and although we all admire the Doctor's weekly letters, yet if he could write it over again we think he would cut it out.


Speaking about writing reminds me of the discussion now going on in regard to our colleges, and the up-to-date education. Did you ever know a boy who, after graduating, come home and went to farming? Unless our population increases very rapidly in the future the question will be, what to do with our graduates. After all the professions are filled up, and school houses provided for, and the clerkships in the stores are filled, what will you do with the graduate? He must live and if his family is unable to support him, and he refuses to plow, and is too proud to beg, we will have a problem on our hands that will even up with the race question. After a boy learns to part his hair in the middle and wear fine clothes all the week as well as Sunday, it does seem like it is almost too hard to ask him to step down from among the clouds and kiss mother earth, especially since the institution once known as Daddyism has disappeared from amongst us. Something, I hope, will turn up to relieve the situation. We have been confronted with many serious problems since the war and have managed somehow to surmount them all, and there is no doubt in my mind but a way will be found to successfully handle our future graduates.


Two of the most notable literary addresses of the season of orations from colleges and church courts one delivered by DR. Moore before the Presbyterian General Assembly in Savannah on the proper education of the child, which every parent should read; and the other by DR. Alderman, of the University of Virginia, being an eulogy of Virginia. It is so different from the usual eulogies of its kind in style, in the manner of handling the subject, in sentiment and in the general flavor of its real literary excellence, that it places the speaker in the foremost rank of America's greatest orators. I should think that every Virginian would want to read it. Speaking of Virginia brings to the mind of most old veterans the stirring days of '61-'65, when she was almost one continuous camping ground of the contending hosts. If every old soldier would give his experiences of the war, and if those notes were used by an expert in history, what a interesting volume could be gotten up. Of course, private men are expected to know nothing about the movements of troops, and orders of battle, etc., but there are a thousand things that come up in the ordinary movement and arrangement of troops before and during battle, and in camp life, that are interesting, instructive and amusing; and if all such data could be assimilated, arranged and blue penciled in form and shape, a readable book could be produced.

regretted. But that fight has yielded
practical results, since the House accept-

"I am sorry to say that Kelley Masson's long memory hen is dead," said Packy Griswold of Hammondsport, N. Y. She was 10 years old and lived on Kelley's vineyard farm in the town of Pultney in old Steuben.

The first brood the hen ever hatched was from a setting of duck eggs. She was very fond of that first family of hers, and they were only a few days old when she strolled with them proudly through the vineyard toward the lake at the foot of the vineyard.

The ducklings no sooner came in sight of the water than they toddled toward it, unmindful of the frantic calls of their hen mother or her distress. They plunged into the lake and were at once having the time of their small lives. By and by, seeing that no harm came to her brood in the water, the hen trotted down soon seemed to be enjoying the antics of the ducklings in the lake as much as they were themselves.

Every day after that the hen escorted her brood to the lake and stood by and watched them sporting in the water with as plain evidences of enjoyment of the scene as animals could give. She continued to take this pleasure every day until the ducks were grown.

The next spring this hen was set on eggs of her own kind. Everybody about the place had forgotten the episode of the ducklings, but it was recalled wildly when the hen, the very first thing she did when she got about with her new brood, led it straightway to the lake.

Her surprise was palpable when none of the family showed any disposition to go into the water, and she tried to coax them in. Not succeeding in that, she picked up one of the chicks in her bill and dropped it into the lake. She stood and watched its struggles in the water until the little thing drowned.

That seemed to be a disappointment to her. She pondered over the matter a while and then picked up another chick and dropped it in the lake. That chick of course struggled in the same way and soon died.

She grabbed another chick and tossed it into the water and threw another in right after it. She was evidently determined to dump the whole disappointing brood into the lake, but her owner thought the sacrifice to the hen's memory had gone far enough and he rescued the remainder of the brood.

That hen hatches a brood of chickens every year. Not once has she failed to lead it to the lake and try to get it to go into the water, ending up by grabbing a chick and teasing it in, when she would be corralled and shut up again.

So Kelley Masson's long memory hen came to be a regular thing to refer to.

I was giving the record of the hen to a New York man who was in Hammondsport the other day and he was anxious to go see her, as it was about time for her to have another brood on hand to exercise that memory of hers.

Kelley is an awful busy man just at that time of year and wouldn't care to be bothered with taking anybody down to his vineyard to see the hen, but the New York man was persistent and I went with him to the store to see if Kelley would do it.

"By jocks, Packy," said Kelley; "it is too bad, but you're too late to have me see the long memory hen!"

"What's the matter?" said I.

"She's dead!" said Kelley. "Died this spring."

"Heinzman," said he abruptly, "my partner wants to raise $4,000 for his personal use. I have agreed to get him that money from the firm."

"Proceed," said Heinzman shrewdly. "As security in case he cannot pay the notes the firm will have to give, he has signed an agreement to turn over to me his undivided one-half interest in our enterprise."

"Well? You want to borrow money of me?" asked Heinzman. "I could not raise it."

"I know that perfectly well," replied Newmark coolly. "You are going to have difficulty meeting your July notes as it is."

Heinzman hardly seemed to breathe, but red blazed in his eye.

"I intend," went on Newmark, "to furnish this money myself. It must, however, seem to be loaned by another. Want you to lend this money on mortgage?"

"What for?" asked Heinzman.

"For a one-tenth of Orde's share in case he does not meet those notes."

"But he will meet the notes," objected Heinzman. "You are a prosperous concern. I know something of your business also."

"He thinks he WILL," rejoined Newmark grimly. "I will mercy point out to you that his entire income is from the firm and that from this income he must save twenty odd thousand a year."

"But the firm has hard luck," said Heinzman.

"Exactly," finished Newmark.

"If you come to me," demanded Heinzman at length.

"Well, I'm offering you a chance to get even with Orde. Don't imagine you love him."

"With you, too?" cried Heinzman. "Ain't you beat me out at Lansing?"

Newmark smiled coldly under his clipped mustache. "I'm offering you the chance of making anywhere from thirty to fifty thousand dollars."

"Perhaps. And suppose this fiddle scheme don't work out."

"And," pursued Newmark calmly, "I'll carry you over in your present obligations." He suddenly hit the arm of his chair with his clinched fist. "Heinzman, if you don't make those July payments what's to become of you? Where's your timber and your mills and your new house and that pretty daughter of yours?"

Heinzman winked visibly.

"It will get an extension of time," said he feebly.

"Will it you?" contemned Newmark.

"Well, maybe," laughed Heinzman uneasily. "It looks to me like winner."

"All right, then," said Newmark briskly. "I'll make out mortgage at 10 per cent for you, and you'll lend the money on it. At the proper time, if things happen that way, you will foreclose. That's all you have to do with it. Then when the timberland comes to you under foreclosure you will reconvey an undivided nine-tenths interest—for proper consideration, of course, and without recording the deed."

Heinzman laughed with assumed lightness. "Suppose I fool you," said he. "I guess I'll just keep it for myself."

Newmark looked at him coldly. "I wouldn't," he advised. "You may remember the member from Lee county in that charter fight and $500 for his vote. Try it on and see how much evidence I can bring up. It's called bribery in this state and it means penitentiary usually."

"You don't take a joke," complained Heinzman.

Newmark arose. "Is it understood, then?" he asked.

"How so? I know you play fair," asked the German.

"You don't. It's a case where we have to depend more or less on each other. But don't see what you stand to lose, and anyway you'll get carried over those July payments," Newmark reminded him.

Heinzman was plainly uneasy. "If you reduce the firm's profits, Orde is going to suspect," he admonished.

"Who said anything about reducing the firm's profits?" said Newmark impatiently. "If it does work out that way, we'll win big. If it does not, we'll lose nothing."

He nodded to Heinzman and left the office. As he entered the office of his own firm his eye fell on Orde's bulk form. He paused involuntarily, and a slight shudder shook his frame—the dainty, instructive repulsion of one for a large, robustious dog. Controlling himself, he stepped forward.

"I've made the loan," he announced. "The banks wouldn't touch northern peninsula, so I had to go to private individuals."

"Don't care who deals it out," laughed Orde.

"Thayer backed out, so finally I got the whole amount from Heinzman," Newmark announced.

"I didn't know he was friend enough to lend us money."

"Business is business," replied Newmark.

one remaining Eskimo made the rest
of the distance alone. Having reached

taking observations. Leaving on the
return journey on April 5, the party
arrived at Cape Columbia on April 10.

Details gleaned from members of the
expedition tell of the long march north,
with party after party dropping out
and turning back to insure a safe re-
treat, until only the chief and his one
attendant were left.

a series of observations were taken
at 90. Peary deposited his records and

perature was 80 degrees below zero

ing, but got no bottom at 1,900 fath-
oms.

packing the sledges, a fact that per-
mitted Marvin to get a good start on

ice was broken about twenty-five yards

the ice where the Eskimos had left
them. The superstitions of their race
prevented the natives from bringing
the dead man's effects with them. Pro-

Washington, November 8

MOTOR VEHICLES ARE UNTRUSTWORTHY.—The army depot commissary on duty in New York City has recommended the use of a travelling kitchen to supply hot foods to troops on the march and the use of auto-vehicles on the line of communication, supplemented by escort wagons on duty with troops. They have come to the conclusion that while the auto vehicle is of value in certain directions and under some conditions, chief reliance must be placed on the ordinary escort wagon. It would not do to depend entirely on motor transportation, partly because of inevitable interruptions of such kind and partly on account of the roughness of country over which military supplies are destined to be carried.

It is appreciated, however, that in future warfare the troops are likely to be concentrated at large camps which must be conveniently located with relation to railroad facilities. When troops are separated from such camps in time of action according to the conservative military view, dependence must be placed upon the vehicles drawn by horses or mules, instead of those propelled by motor. There is also some doubt as to the need of travelling kitchen, in addition to the existing facilities for providing sufficiently well cooked food for the soldier who is not supplied from the garrison or camp kitchen. To hold the trains down to a minimum, in order that the mobility of troops in time of war may not be seriously impeded, must be regarded as of first importance. Some consideration has been given to the travelling kitchen by the commissary general of the army who has had tested under practical conditions such devices as are used in the European armies, and the conclusion has been reached that the benefits do not offset the disadvantages.

the Glenwood Avalanche to the effect

Central Colorado Power company from

denied in a letter from General Manager
G. H. Walbridge to the Glenwood

December 2.

one of the many reports set afloat,

facts or downright desire to in some

cessfully that which the doubting ones
were but yesterday saying was impos-

across the great Continental Divide
and to the city of Denver and there
use the juice in driving the big
company. But that which has been done
is wonderful as it may seem.

itudes. Substations along the lines,
equipped with recording instruments

open, and as an additional safeguard,
riders are employed to patrol the route
followed. Three copper transmission
cables and an iron ground cable in-
tended to protect the transmission

The subjects of industrial insurance, state aid for highways and the income tax may be investigated by committees and considered at a short session called by the governor in about a year.

Commission Form Of Government.

Among the bills already drafted by the legislative reference library at the request of the legislators is bill to give Wisconsin cities the option of adopting the commission form of government now in operation in nine different states. So favorably has the plan been received in Madison that a meeting of citizens has been called for this evening to banquet and discuss the advisability of asking the legislature to pass such a law. The plan was defeated two years ago when presented by Senator Noble, but further experience with the system in this country, and particularly at Des Moines, has created more sentiment for it.

The bill will provide for the abolition of the present common councils and the election at large of five commissioners who act in both legislative and executive capacities. It also provides for recall if any member is unsatisfactory.

social considerations of the modern

man is the space problem. Unlike

our grandfathers, we unfortunately

do not live in houses that have large

makes the clothes storage question

ideas, however, have reduced the space

across the inside of the closet, usually

below the shelves and extending from

wall to wall, though there are some

excellent variations from this prin-

ciple.

latter type comprises a notched arm

extending at right angles from the

closet door or wall with a notch

for each hanger so that each one can

take up only just so much space and

can never encroach on that of its

neighbor.

Washington, Jan. 8.—The house committees having in charge the various appropriation bills are busily occupied with hearings and meetings for the consideration of those bills in all effort to report them to the house at the earliest possible moment. The committee on naval affairs and the agricultural committee are holding hearings on the bills to provide funds for those two important departments. A subcommittee of the foreign affairs committee took up this week for consideration the estimates for appropriations required for foreign intercourse during the next fiscal year. The committees on military affairs and on rivers and harbors will each consider the bills required for the work with which they are identified.

The committee on rivers and harbors held a meeting on Tuesday to consider the advisability of bringing in a river and harbor bill at this session of congress, but no conclusion was reached. Another meeting will be held on Friday, when it will be decided. Owing to the pressure being brought upon the present congress, the appropriations asked for by the respective committees will be of unusual interest.

The special committee appointed to report to the house on the offensive portion of the president's annual message regarding the secret service are having a hard time of it. They are expected to bring into the house on Friday a report which will satisfy the most radical member of congress.

Five distinct propositions are now said to be under consideration—to expunge from the records the offensive remarks of the annual message; to lay the annual message on the table indefinitely; to return the message to the president without comment; to return the message with the objections of the house enumerated; to return the special message of explanation with the blunt statement that it is irrelevant and that it does not satisfactorily explain the charges previously made by the president.

It is said that personally the president isn't in the slightest degree concerned with what the house may do, by way of censuring him or otherwise expressing displeasure. He has asked all the members of his cabinet to make a report to him of the uses made by them of the secret service in times past, and will send them to the senate at once. Chicago, Sept. 14.—Extreme dullness prevailed in the wheat market early last week, but popular sentiment veered strongly to the bull side after the opening Tuesday and the bulls in the trade continued to increase as the week progressed. Much of the bullishness was based on the stubborn fact that wheat has recently failed to decline under heavy selling pressure, but has proven much more responsive to buying. Part of this sentiment was also based on the assumption that Russia, now an enormous shipper, will soon be out of the market. Failure of the European centers, however, to become excited over the Russian figures rather indicates that importing nations are skeptical about the Russian short crop claims. In the event that they prove true Europe would undoubtedly be in the Canadian and United States markets as a buyer of wheat on a very large scale. There has been no indication of any such development during the week just ended, and, until an export demand develops, many conservative grain men will go slow in indorsing an upward movement of wheat prices in this country. Meanwhile the scarcity of soft winter wheat is so pronounced that prices at the strictly soft winter markets, St. Louis and Toledo, are now higher than at Liverpool for similar grades.


More or less Unloading.


The best advance of the week was made on Friday when it became apparent that the September delivery was much congested. Smaller shorts became almost panic-stricken, but the leading longs finally let enough wheat to prevent a general stampede of September shorts. More or less early unloading was done by December and May longs among the leading room traders because of the disappointment over the Liverpool cables. This started a selling move among miscellaneous pit traders.

Last evening President Taft and large
audience of thoroughly contented play
goers went through a course of rejuvena-
tion, together with Miss May Robson,
who, in the character of Aunt Mary, was
being taught the advantages of the
modern wiry by her nephew and his ac-
commodating friend. All came through
the ordeal with credit—the players, whose
work was very worthy of praise, and the
audience, which never forgot to laugh at

occurred with alarming rapidity, so that
each auditor was kept keenly alive to
the responsibilities of his position.

been seen in Washington before, so it
needs no introduction to the public, but
it is very pleasant to record that in the
interim it has broken all traditions, and
really improved. Last evening's perform-
ance was as fresh, and given with as
much dash, as though it were the first

to meet us and led the way to the
caves, which were completely hid
den by thicket. On the rocky plat
form in front of the cave the men all
surrounded us shouting to their wom-
en—to come and see their white sis-
ter-in-law or cousin Veddas have
fulness, and this reputation we are
able to indorse. Each community has
its own hunting ground, and adheres
strictly to its own game rights. Upon
each hunting ground there are num-
ber of caves and rock shelters, and the
families of the community move from
one to another throughout the year,
as the presence of game, honey, yams
or fish demands. The big caves are
communal property, the smaller caves
usually belong to single families; but
even in the communal caves each fam-
ily has its particular place in which its
members sleep, cook, eat and keep all
their belongings.

Each family respects the pri-
vacy of its neighbors' few feet of the
cave floor as faithfully as if partition
walls existed; only the children roam
all over the cave at will. Food, how-
ever, seemed to be public property, for
one woman would cook food and share
it with every one present in the cave.
This may probably be explained as
follows: The communal caves are sit-
uated in common hunting ground;
therefore all the game, vans, iguanas
or honey brought in from the COM-
mon land is the property of the COM-
munity, not of the man who pro-
cures it.

I have stated that the smaller
caves are usually private property. It
would probably be more correct to say
that Veddas possess private hunting
grounds on which very frequently
there are small caves, such caves be-
ing then the property of the owner
of the land. When a man is living
in his own cave in the midst of his
own hunting ground the produce of
the chase would naturally be his own,
though shared with any one living
with him. Women and children al-
ways fared as well as the men, and
the former would be fed first in any
time of scarcity. Indeed, the dainties
were often saved for the children."

TACOMA, March 12.-In the trial
today of the assault charge against
Joshua Klein, the radioactive" phil
osopher, accused of enticing two Ia
coma girls, Miss Sauvegeot and Miss
Karasek, to his chalet in Switzerland
and holding them prisoners with
number Of other women converts, Mrs.
Sauvegeot was recalled to the stand
and told of her trip to Kein's chalet
in Amden, Switzerland. in the attempt
to persuade her daughter to come
home.


At each mention of her daughters
name the woman wept Historically.


She testified she did not believe the
moral atmosphere of the place was
sound. Asked if she had personal rea-
sons for this belief. she flushed, hesi-
tated and appealed to the court for
protection.


The defense Immediately withdrew
the question and thus avoided what
from the beginning of the trial it has
been thought would lead to sensational
disclosures.


Irma, the 17-year- old daughter of
Mrs Sauvegeot, testified to the scene
in the Sauvegeot home on the after
noon when the assault upon her moth
er is said to have taken place. She
declared she heard Klein threaten to
kill her mother and he also asserted
during his furious denunciation of the
woman that he could create a Vfbra-
ton of the atmosphere that would de-
stroy the city of Seattle, thirty miles
away.


During Mrs. Sauvegeot's examina-
ton she asked that Klein be removed
from the court room as he exercised
an influence that almost prevented her
from telling the truth. She thought
he was partially in control of her
mind.


The court refused to remove Klein
from the room.

THE TRIBUNE BUREAU

Washington, Nov. 25.—The progress which has been made in the development of harbor defence by submarine mines in the last few years is hardly realized by any who have not kept in close touch with the administration of the coast defence corps under General Arthur Murray, its chief. Up to a comparatively few years ago this branch of the coast defence had been little developed, and rough estimates of the funds required to bring it up to date called for appallingly large appropriations. By the exercise of energy and ingenuity, however, the coast defence corps has succeeded in developing a system of submarine defence at reasonable expense.

The first problem which confronted the officers charged with this class of work was to secure an adequate number of vessels with which to teach the system and to perform the work of mine planting. Congress has been induced to provide eight large mine planting vessels, available for educational purposes as well for the actual work. Four of these are now maintained on the Atlantic Coast, two on the Pacific Coast, and two in the Philippines. In addition seventeen smaller vessels have been provided.

The most carefully scaled estimates showed the necessity of at least forty additional vessels for time of war. Apart from the cost of construction, these vessels would have caused an annual expense for maintenance of probably $1,500,000, and it not deemed wise to ask Congress for the necessary funds. In order to meet this difficulty, however, General Murray prevailed on the Secretary of Commerce and Labor to designate thirty-one lighthouse tenders for use as mine planters in the event of hostilities, and the quartermaster's department to designate ten of its vessels for a similar purpose. This much accomplished, the necessary paraphernalia for mine planting were manufactured and fitted to the vessels so designated, and the necessary means of attachment, such as sockets, etc., placed thereon, but the machinery itself is stored in suitable warehouses in the districts in which these vessels are stationed, as are also the mines which they would plant should the occasion arise. By this method the coast artillery is saved the cost of maintenance for forty-one vessels which would however be immediately available should the occasion demand.

For many years the proposition laid down by General Abbott that water more than one hundred feet deep or having a current greater than seven feet a second could not be successfully mined has been accepted without question. By experiments conducted by General Murray and Major Richmond A. Davis in the Race, at the eastern end of Long Island Sound, an automatic anchor has been perfected which overcomes difficulties caused both by depth of water and by current. Mines have been successfully anchored in the Race in water three hundred feet deep in such manner as to maintain them just ten feet below the surface and practically stationary. The necessary supplies for mining most of the harbors of the United States have been constructed and stored in suitable buildings at convenient points. About five thousand officers and men have been thoroughly drilled in the work of mine planting.

The system of mine protection has been so far developed that the mines—each contains about 125 pounds of gun-cotton, when planted—are connected by electric cables with a casemate on shore, within fortifications, and usually below ground, and can be operated by any one of three methods. By the adjustment of an electric switch they can be made to explode on contact with any vessel that touches them, a further turn of the switch will cause any mine touched by a vessel to indicate the fact by the lighting of a electric bulb when it can be exploded by the pressure of a button. Finally, any one of a group of mines can be exploded at the judgment of the battle commander by further adjustment of the switch and the pressure of a button.

Experiments already made have demonstrated the feasibility of effectively mining Manila and Subic Bay, and work is now going forward with view to devising practical system of mine protection for the swift waters of San Francisco Bay. The problem of mining Puget Sound, where the current is extraordinarily swift and the great depth makes even the anchoring of naval vessels difficult, will next be undertaken.

CHICAGO, Sept. 24.—Otto T. Barnard, who was nominated as the Republican candidate for Mayor of New York last night, arrived here to-day to attend the wedding of his niece.

"I obviously cannot enter upon a detailed account of my position at this moment," said Mr. Barnard. "I have not been officially notified of my nomination; have not had the opportunity to study the platform which was adopted; and Tammany has not shown its hand regarding the candidate for Mayor and its proposed course of action, and the Independent forces, which, if they will support me, have not had the chance to declare their position. All that I can say with regard to the campaign is that I have informed Mr. Parsons and the Republican leaders in New York that they can count on me to make the most determined sort of fight which is within my power."

"In a general way," he added, "the issue in New York is simple. It seems to be merely a question as to the ability of Tammany Hall to govern an administration which has been a disgrace to the city. New York has the chance to put Tammany down and out."

Mr. Barnard said that his advices from New York were that his nomination would prove satisfactory to all the anti-Tammany elements, with the Hearst forces, of course, being an exception.

"I have been and am now an organization Republican. The Hearst representative quit the conference committee when we were attempting to agree to a ticket and declaration of principles. In the face of his withdrawal, considering the reasons which he expressed, it is difficult to imagine his supporting me. There is no political or practical possibility that the Hearst interests can support the Tammany nominee, whomsoever he may be. The Hearst people may have to go it alone, in which case Mr. Hearst might become a candidate for Mayor himself. Stranger things have happened in New York."

HAS LITTLE FEAR OF GAYNOR.

"Personally, I should welcome a duel between Justice Gaynor, as the Tammany nominee, and myself. I would have little fear of the result in that case. Murphy may not name Justice Gaynor. His only reason, the political leaders understand, is that Tammany throws support to Brooklyn, in the expectation of securing the rest of the ticket and the control of the Board of Estimate, which is all that Tammany wants and all that Tammany ever has wanted.

"The real issue is down to one big dominating point: Is Tammany to be permitted to continue its control of the contracts through the Estimate Board, and is the patronage of the Comptroller's office to remain the chief asset of the Tammany organization?"

Mr. Barnard did not wish to give his views in detail. He said that to do so at this time would not be fair to himself or to the convention which nominated him.

"All I can say at this time," he said, "is that it is my purpose to stand on the platform which the Republican convention formulated. I am advised from New York that I need have no fear in making such a statement, although I have not yet had the opportunity of reading the declaration of principles."

Mr. Barnard said that his return to New York on Tuesday would open the campaign so far as he was personally concerned, but that, due to the festivities incident to the Hudson-Fulton celebration, active work would not be undertaken until some time later.

"I presume, of course, that my connection with the New York Trust Company will be used as a campaign argument," said Mr. Barnard. "That might have been expected. That institution is not in the control of any financial clique or of any particular group of financial interests, and certainly it is not controlled by any railroad or traction interests."

"What do you think of the ticket nominated by the Republican convention?"

PRAISES THE TICKET

"It is an excellent ticket, in my judgment," said Mr. Barnard. "The nomination of Mr. [unintelligible] Democrat for President of the Board of Estimate seems to me to be a fitting recognition, such as to assure to the ticket strong support from the heavy independent anti-Tammany vote, which is absolutely necessary in order to defeat Tammany. Under conditions that exist while Tammany Hall is in power, it is a practical physical impossibility for a city to win out."

Mr. Barnard said his information led him to believe that the Republican organization will be vastly united behind the ticket he heads. He was informed by telegram from Mr. Parsons, "The train arrived at Syracuse. You have made the nominee by unanimous vote." He said since the beginning that all of the party elements are in thorough harmony, and that they intend to enter the campaign strongly. He added, "We have reason to believe that the independent bodies which have been working on the opposition to disrupting the power of Tammany are in line with us."

"I was not expected to be nominated, and was greatly surprised at the word from the convention. I had been at the convention during the whole session, but without any anticipation that I would be nominated. Of course, talk that 'New York is a joke' had to come to Chicago for the marriage of my niece for many weeks."

Mr. Barnard's niece, Miss Florence Barnard, will be married to Francis Adams, Jr., tomorrow night at the home of Mr. and Mrs. J. Barnard, No. 59 Bellevue Place. Mr. Adams is the son of Judge Francis Adams. Mr. Barnard will go to Milwaukee on Sunday morning with his father, who is eighty-eight years old, and they will take the Twentieth Century Limited from New York on Monday afternoon.

It is hereby ordered, That, commencing on the 1st day of October, 1908, the postage rate applicable to letters mailed in United States, addressed for delivery at any place in the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, shall be two (2) cents an ounce or fraction of an ounce.

Postmaster General.


Behind this simple statement is a vast amount of Republican constructive legislation which resulted in the significant accomplishment, set forth by the Postmaster General. It is eloquently prophetic of a worldwide penny postage, for which the credit will be due to a Republican administration.


Sixth Universal Postal Congress.


The Sixth Universal Postal Congress convened in the city of Rome, Italy, April 7 and continued until May 20, 1905. Sixty-five countries, including the United States, were represented. The assembly was for the purpose of discussing the postal systems of all nations and, if possible, agreeing upon measures for the improvement in all practical ways, of the regulations governing mails. The first congress of this kind met in Berne, Switzerland, in 1874.


The United States Post Office Department was represented in this World Postal Congress by two delegates—the Superintendent of Division of Foreign Mails, as in previous postal congresses, and the Hon. Edward Water of the Omaha Bee, who also served in the preceding postal congress.


Move for Universal Penny Postage.


At this Universal Postal Congress representatives of the United States proposed a universal two-cent postage to all nations. The Hon. J. Henniker Heaton, M.P., who is the father of the two-cent idea in England, speaking of America's action at the Rome convention, in standing out for a universal two-cent postal rate, said:


"The British members stood coldly by. They did not recognize that this was a great historic occasion, a worthy parallel of that solemn scene on July 4, 1776, when the Declaration of Independence was adopted; for if the Americans are willing to adopt penny postage to all parts of the world, it follows that they are willing to establish it to the British Empire and form a 'Restrictive Postal Union.'"


The Hon. Whitelaw Reid, America's Republican minister to the court of St. James, praised the work of the American delegation and solicited the friendly cooperation of the British government at a Fourth of July banquet speech in London in 1906. Mr. Reid said:


"The American people hoped for closer and cheaper communications with all other nations as the best means of promoting better acquaintance and perpetuating friendship. They were gratified to find that the British apostle of penny postage (Mr. Heaton) at this moment focusing his efforts on what ought to be the easy task of persuading the authorities on both sides of the Atlantic, that it was as cheap to carry a letter from London to New York as from London to Calcutta or from New York to Manila—and quite as useful."


American Republicans Lead the Way


So it has come to pass that the United States, under its Republican administration, is entering into a convention with Great Britain whereby after the 1st of October, this year, a two-cent postage rate will obtain between this country and England, Ireland, Scotland and Wales. We already have such an arrangement with Canada, Mexico, Cuba, Panama and our colonial possessions. This great accomplishment is universally recognized as the proper beginning which is to result in a universal two-cent postage rate around the world.


Important Things Accomplished


Two other important things that the Republican administration accomplished at the Rome Universal Postal Congress through its representatives, must not be lost sight of. One was the adoption of a universal return coupon stamp. In exchange for which, upon presentation at a post office in another country, the person presenting it shall receive a postage stamp of the value of 8 cents, good in any country of the world, thus enabling people here to prepay postage at regular rates upon reply letters.


The other significant concession was that in all World Postal Congresses to be held in the future, the United States is to be granted an additional vote.

An Aeroplane, and Meets Success
fully the Final Test.

A special dispatch from Washington says last Friday evening Orville Wright attained the zenith of hard earned success. In ten mile cross-country flight in the famous aeroplane, built by himself and his elder brother, Wilbur, and accompanied by Lieut. Benjamin Foulois, an intrepid officer of the army signal corps, he not only surpassed the speed requirements of his contract with the United States government, but accomplished the most difficult and daring flight ever planned for a heavier-than-air flying machine. Incidentally he broke all speed records over measured course. And he established beyond dispute the practicability of an aeroplane in time of peace and in time of war.

His speed was over 42 miles an hour; he made the ten-mile flight from Fort Myer and back in 14 minutes and forty-two seconds, including the more than twenty seconds required for the turn beyond the line at Shutter Hill, the southern end of the course. He attained a height in crossing the valley of Four Mile Run of nearly 500 feet, and the average altitude of his practically level course was about 200 feet above the ground.

President Taft, who had become an enthusiastic spectator of the aeroplane trials, although two years ago when Secretary of War, he is said to have expressed to officers profound scepticism as to the accomplishment of such a feat as that of which he saw the completion, arrived upon the parade grounds at Fort Myer just in time to see the aeroplane land and to participate in the wild demonstration which welcomed the triumphant aviators. He sent an officer to bear his congratulations to the victors.

A terrific wind and rain storm early in the afternoon seemed providentially provided - clear and quiet the atmospheric conditions in preparation for the flight, which was delayed only by the failure of the army field telegraph line from Fort Myer to Shutter Hill. It was still out of commission when Orville Wright, seizing the moment of the best weather conditions he had yet had for the speed test, had the machine placed on the starting rail and gave the motor a final test.

The engine worked perfectly, and the crowd seemed to realize that an epoch-making moment was at hand. They pressed forward against the lines, which held them back breathless, intense, eagerly watching every movement of the aviator and his machine. The signal corps detail hoisted the great weight in the starting derrick which gives the machine its initial impulse.

Lieut. Foulois, lithe, wiry, brown as a berry, in his khaki uniform and leggings, at a sign from Orville, climbed into the passenger's seat beside the motor. Wilbur and Charley Taylor, the Wrights' mechanic, took their places at the propellers. Orville turned on the sparker of the motor, and they whirled the blades around. The motor picked up the impetus, Orville turned on the speed, and for the first time the propellers of the Wright aeroplane were whirling at their maximum capacity.

The smooth and even song of the engine aroused the crowd to excited cheering. Orville clambered into his seat and gripped the levers. Wilbur, at a nod from his brother, slipped the cable which released the weight, the aeroplane shot down the track, rose before it reached the end, and skinned over the surface of the ground for a hundred feet or more.

As if drawn up by invisible powers, the white-winged man-bird rose higher and higher, reached the end and faced about, climbing up as it were on the air higher and yet higher. Orville brought the machine at great speed once again fully round the field. Then with a short turn he evened about and started southward over the center of the drill field.

"They're Off," a thousand voices shouted as one.

Like a giant bird circling its prey, this man-bird then darted off toward Shutter Hill, five miles to the south.

Unwavering it kept its straight course, and seemed to be rising ever higher, as it passed over the diverse and heavily wooded country in the distance. Soon it was a mere speck against the pearl sky above.

CHAPTER 40, LAWS OF 1908.
AN ACT relating to the aggregate funded debt of cities of the first class.

The people of the state of Wisconsin, represented in Senate and Assembly, do enact as follows:

Section 1. The principal of the aggregate funded debt of cities of the first class shall never exceed a sum equal to five per centum on the amount of the assessed value of the taxable property in any such city, which value shall be ascertained and determined by the average annual amount on the assessment rolls thereof for the preceding five years; and all bonds hereafter issued by any such city shall contain a covenant to that effect, and all bonds, notes or other evidences of debt, payable on a future day, which shall be issued by any such city contrary to this section, and in excess of the limitation herein prescribed, either with or without statutory authority, shall be void; provided, that the foregoing limitation shall not apply to or include orders drawn upon the city treasurer, payable out of the revenue of the current year; and provided, further, that the common council may borrow from time to time upon the notes of the city, signed by the mayor and city comptroller, such sums of money in anticipation of the incoming revenue of the year as they shall deem necessary to pay accruing interest on the funded debt and to meet the current expenses of the city, and all such notes shall be paid out of the taxes of the current year at such time as may be agreed on—not later than the first day of February next following the date; and provided, further, that nothing herein contained shall be held to abrogate or impair, modify or repeal the provisions of section one of chapter two hundred and fifty-two of the laws of 1893 or of section one of chapter two hundred and fifty-five of the laws of 1890 or of section nine hundred and forty-one of the statutes of 1881.

II. In any case, any such city or any officer of such city shall hereafter threaten or attempt to issue any such bonds, notes, or other evidences of debt contrary to the provisions of this section, they shall be restrained by injunction from so doing, upon the application of any holder of bonds of the said city, or of any citizen who has paid city taxes in said city for the three years then preceding.

Section 2. This act shall take effect and be in force from and after its passage and publication.

Approved June 11, 1909.

Richmond, Va. May l4.--In a
session that was at times stormy
and turbulent, the democratic state
central committee tonight fixed
August as the date for the hold
ing of the gubernatorial primary;
settled upon the assessment to be
lain upon the candidates; declined
to accept the temporary reslgna-
ton of Chairman Ellyson, who is
candidate for reelection as lieuten-
ant governor, and referred the
question of amending the primary
plan to IA subcommittee, with in
structions to seport back to the
next meeting of the full committee.


The present primary system was
bombarded from many quarters,
and if the applause which greets
the attacks upon it, conveys q fair
idea of the sentiment. it is not pop
ular, by any means, with the party
leaders.


An attempt was made to get a
resolution through, calling for a
state convention to frame a party
platform, but it was tabled by an
overwhelming majority,


The body was called to order by
Secretary BRENNAN, with Edward
Echols, of Staunton, in the chair,
in the absence of the regular chair
man, who had sent a message to
the body, that as he was a candi-
date for ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS, he
did not think it wise for him to
preside. In a moment resolution
followed appointing committee to
call Mr.. Ellyson to the room as the
presiding officer. He was forth
with called and presented, and Mr..
Echols retired.


A matter of important discussion
was the amount of assessment re-
quired from each candidate. The
amount needed was estimated at
So. 900, This was apportioned as
follows: To enter race for senate,
81 500; governor, 81 500; lieuten-
ant governor, $500; attorney gen.
eral, $500; treasurer, $500; secre--
tary of the commonwealth, $500;
superintendent of public instruc-
